danish.title: Syvende bog (1810–11) — Kapitel 8
paragraphs: Grev Iljá Rostov havde nedlagt sin post som adelsmarskalk, fordi den kostede ham for meget, men alligevel forbedredes deres økonomi ikke. Natásha og Nikolaj lagde ofte mærke til, at deres forældre samtalede ængsteligt og hemmeligt og hørte antydninger om at sælge det smukke gamle Rostov-hus og godset nær Moskva. Det var ikke nødvendigt at holde så mange selskaber, som da greven havde været marskalk, og livet i Otrádnoe var roligere end i tidligere år. Men alligevel var det enorme hus med tilbygningerne fuldt af mennesker, og mere end tyve satte sig til bords hver dag. Det var alt sammen deres egne folk, der havde slået sig ned i huset nærmest som familiemedlemmer, eller personer, der, syntes det, var nødt til at bo i grevens hus. Sådanne var musikeren Dimmler og hans hustru, dansemesteren Vogel og hans familie, Belóva, en gammel ugift dame og fast beboer, og mange andre som Petjas huslærere, pigernes tidligere guvernante og andre folk, der simpelthen fandt det at foretrække og mere fordelagtigt at bo i grevens hus end hjemme. De havde ikke så mange gæster som før, men de gamle vaner, uden hvilke greven og grevinden ikke kunne forestille sig tilværelsen, bestod uændret. Der var stadig jagtetablissementet, som Nikolaj endda havde udvidet, de samme halvtreds heste og femten staldkarle, de samme kostbare gaver og middage for hele distriktet på navnedage; der var stadig grevens whist- og bostonspil, hvor han — med kortene spredt ud, så alle kunne se dem — lod sig plyndre for hundreder af rubler hver dag af sine naboer, der betragtede muligheden for at spille en rubber med grev Rostov som en yderst indbringende indtægtskilde.

Greven bevægede sig i sine forretninger som i et kæmpestort net, idet han forsøgte ikke at tro, at han var viklet ind, men blev mere og mere fanget ved hvert skridt og følte sig for svag til at bryde maskerne eller til tålmodigt og omhyggeligt at rede dem ud. Grevinden, der med sit kærlige hjerte følte, at hendes børn blev ødelagt, at det ikke var grevens skyld, for han kunne ikke gøre for, hvad han var — at han selv (skønt han forsøgte at skjule det) led under bevidstheden om sin egen og sine børns ruin, forsøgte at finde midler til at rette op på stillingen. Fra sit kvindelige synspunkt kunne hun kun se én løsning: at Nikolaj giftede sig med en rig arving. Hun følte, at dette var deres sidste håb, og at hvis Nikolaj afslog det parti, hun havde fundet til ham, ville hun måtte opgive ethvert håb om nogen sinde at bringe sagerne i orden. Dette parti var med Julie Karágina, datter af fortræffelige og dydige forældre, en pige, familien Rostov havde kendt fra barnsben, og som nu var blevet en rig arving efter den sidste af hendes brødres død.

Grevinden havde skrevet direkte til Julies mor i Moskva og foreslået et ægteskab mellem deres børn og modtaget et gunstigt svar. Karágina svarede, at hun for sin del var indforstået, og at alt afhang af datterens tilbøjelighed. Hun indbød Nikolaj til at komme til Moskva.

Flere gange fortalte grevinden med tårer i øjnene sin søn, at nu da begge hendes døtre var etablerede, var hendes eneste ønske at se ham gift. Hun sagde, at hun kunne lægge sig i sin grav med ro, hvis det blev opfyldt. Så fortalte hun ham, at hun kendte en strålende pige, og forsøgte at finde ud af, hvad han tænkte om ægteskab.

Andre gange roste hun Julie for ham og rådede ham til at tage til Moskva i ferien og more sig. Nikolaj gættede, hvad hans mors bemærkninger sigtede mod, og under en af disse samtaler fik han hende til at tale rent ud. Hun fortalte ham, at hendes eneste håb om at få deres sager bragt i orden nu lå i, at han giftede sig med Julie Karágina.

»Men, mama — antag at jeg elskede en pige uden formue, ville du så forvente, at jeg ofrede mine følelser og min ære for pengenes skyld?« spurgte han sin mor, uden at indse grusomheden i sit spørgsmål og kun ønskende at vise sin ædelhed.

»Nej, du har ikke forstået mig,« sagde moderen, der ikke vidste, hvordan hun skulle retfærdiggøre sig. »Du har ikke forstået mig, Nikólenka. Det er din lykke, jeg ønsker,« tilføjede hun, idet hun følte, at hun talte usandt og blev mere og mere viklet ind. Hun begyndte at græde.
»Mama, græd ikke! Sig mig blot, at du ønsker det, og du ved, at jeg vil give mit liv, alt, for at berolige dig,« sagde Nikolaj. »Jeg ville ofre alt for dig — selv mine følelser.«
Men grevinden ønskede ikke, at spørgsmålet blev stillet sådan; hun ønskede ikke et offer fra sin søn — hun ønskede selv at bringe et offer for ham.
»Nej, du har ikke forstået mig — lad os ikke tale om det,« svarede hun og tørrede sine tårer.

»Måske elsker jeg virkelig en fattig pige,« sagde Nikolaj til sig selv. »Skal jeg ofre mine følelser og min ære for penge? Jeg undrer mig over, at mama kunne tale sådan til mig. Fordi Sonja er fattig, skal jeg så ikke elske hende,« tænkte han, »skal jeg ikke svare på hendes trofaste, hengivne kærlighed? Og dog ville jeg bestemt være lykkeligere med hende end med en eller anden dukkeagtig Julie. Jeg kan altid ofre mine følelser for familiens vel,« sagde han til sig selv, »men mine følelser kan jeg ikke kommandere. Hvis jeg elsker Sonja, er den følelse for mig stærkere og højere end alt andet.«

Nikolaj tog ikke til Moskva, og grevinden genoptog ikke samtalen om ægteskab med ham. Med sorg og undertiden med irritation så hun tegn på en voksende tilknytning mellem sin søn og den medgiftsløse Sonja. Skønt hun bebrejdede sig det, kunne hun ikke lade være med at skumle over og chikanere Sonja, idet hun ofte irettesatte hende uden grund, tiltale hende stivt som »min kære« og brugte det formelle De i stedet for det fortrolige du, når hun talte til hende. Den venlige grevinde var des mere irriteret på Sonja, fordi denne stakkels, mørkeøjede niece var så sagtmodig, så god, så hengivent taknemmelig mod sine velgørere og så trofast, uforanderligt og uselvisk forelsket i Nikolaj, at der ingen grund var til at finde fejl ved hende.

Nikolaj tilbragte den sidste del af sin orlov hjemme. Et fjerde brev var kommet fra fyrst Andrej, fra Rom, hvori han skrev, at han for længst ville have været på vej hjem til Rusland, hvis ikke hans sår uventet var brudt op i det varme klima, hvilket nødsagede ham til at udsætte sin hjemkomst til begyndelsen af det nye år. Natásha var stadig lige så forelsket i sin forlovede, fandt den samme trøst i kærligheden og var stadig lige så rede til at kaste sig ud i alle livets glæder som før. Men ved udgangen af den fjerde måned af deres adskillelse begyndte hun at få anfald af tungsind, som hun ikke kunne beherske. Hun havde ondt af sig selv: ondt af, at hun blev spildt hele denne tid og ikke var til nytte for nogen — mens hun følte sig så i stand til at elske og blive elsket.
Det var ikke muntert i familien Rostovs hjem.

english.title: Book Seven (1810 - 11) — Chapter 8
paragraphs: Count Ilya Rostov had given up the position of Provincial Marshal of the Nobility because it cost too much, but their finances had not improved. Natasha and Nicholas often noticed their parents conferring anxiously in private and heard talk of selling the grand ancestral Rostov house and the estate near Moscow. It was no longer necessary to entertain as lavishly as when the count had been Marshal, and life at Otradnoe was quieter than before — but still the enormous house and its wings were full of people, and more than twenty sat down to dinner every day. These were all people who had settled into the house almost as family members, or who seemed, for one reason or another, compelled to live in the count's household. There were Dimmler the musician and his wife, Vogel the dancing master and his family, Belova the elderly spinster who was an established member of the house, and many others — Petya's tutors, the girls' former governess, and people who simply found it more convenient or advantageous to live at the count's expense than at home. They didn't have as many guests as before, but the old habits without which the count and countess couldn't imagine life remained unchanged. There was still the hunting establishment, which Nicholas had even expanded; the same fifty horses and fifteen grooms in the stables; the same expensive gifts and festive dinners for the whole district on name days; the count's card games of whist and boston, at which — laying out his cards so everyone could see them — he let his neighbors plunder him of hundreds of rubles a day, neighbors who considered a rubber with Count Rostov one of their most profitable sources of income.

The count moved through his affairs as through a vast net, trying not to believe he was entangled but getting more deeply caught at every step, and feeling too feeble either to tear through the mesh or to sit down and patiently untangle it. The countess, with her loving heart, sensed that her children were being ruined. It was not the count's fault — he couldn't help being what he was — and he suffered from the awareness of his own and his children's ruin, though he tried to hide it. She tried to find a remedy. From her feminine perspective, she could see only one solution: Nicholas must marry a rich heiress. She felt this was their last hope, and that if Nicholas refused the match she had found for him, she would have to give up any hope of ever setting things right. This match was with Julie Karagina, the daughter of excellent and virtuous parents, a girl the Rostovs had known since childhood and who had recently become a wealthy heiress through the death of her last surviving brother.

The countess had written directly to Julie's mother in Moscow proposing a marriage between their children and had received a favorable reply. Karagina said that for her part she was agreeable, and everything would depend on her daughter's feelings. She invited Nicholas to come to Moscow.

Several times the countess, with tears in her eyes, told her son that now both her daughters were settled, her only wish was to see him married. She said she could rest in peace if that were accomplished. Then she mentioned a wonderful girl and tried to find out what he thought about marriage.

At other times she praised Julie and urged him to go to Moscow during the holidays and enjoy himself. Nicholas guessed what his mother was driving at, and during one of these conversations he got her to speak frankly. She told him that their only hope of untangling the family's finances now lay in his marrying Julie Karagina.

"But, Mama, suppose I loved a girl who has no fortune — would you expect me to sacrifice my feelings and my honor for money?" he asked his mother, not realizing the cruelty of his question and only wanting to demonstrate his own nobility.

"No, you've misunderstood me," said his mother, not knowing how to defend herself. "You've misunderstood me, Nikolenka. It's your happiness I want," she added, feeling she was not being truthful and was getting tangled up. She began to cry.
"Mama, don't cry! Just tell me you want it, and you know I'll give my life — anything — to make you happy," said Nicholas. "I would sacrifice anything for you — even my feelings."
But the countess didn't want the question framed that way: she didn't want a sacrifice from her son — she wanted to sacrifice for him.
"No, you've misunderstood me — let's not talk about it," she said, wiping her tears.

"Maybe I do love a poor girl," Nicholas thought to himself. "Am I supposed to sacrifice my feelings and my honor for money? I wonder how Mama could say such a thing to me. Because Sonya is poor, I mustn't love her," he thought, "mustn't respond to her faithful, devoted love? And yet I'd certainly be happier with her than with some doll-like Julie. I can always sacrifice my feelings for the family's sake," he told himself, "but I can't force my feelings. If I love Sonya, that feeling is, for me, stronger and more sacred than anything."

Nicholas did not go to Moscow, and the countess did not bring up the subject of marriage again. She watched with sorrow and sometimes with anger as signs of a deepening attachment between her son and the penniless Sonya grew ever more evident. Though she blamed herself for it, she couldn't help nagging and needling Sonya, often snapping at her for no reason, addressing her coldly as "my dear" and using the formal "you" instead of the intimate "thou." The kindhearted countess was all the more vexed with Sonya because that poor, dark-eyed niece was so meek, so kind, so devotedly grateful to her benefactors, and so faithfully, unchangingly, and selflessly in love with Nicholas that there were no real grounds for finding fault with her.

Nicholas was spending the last of his leave at home. A fourth letter had arrived from Prince Andrew, this time from Rome, in which he wrote that he would have been on his way back to Russia long ago if his wound had not unexpectedly reopened in the warm climate, forcing him to postpone his return until the beginning of the new year. Natasha was still as much in love with her fiance and found the same comfort in that love, and was still as ready to throw herself into all the pleasures of life as before; but toward the end of the fourth month of their separation she began to have bouts of depression she couldn't master. She felt sorry for herself: sorry that she was being wasted all this time and was no use to anyone — while she felt herself so capable of loving and being loved.
Things were not cheerful in the Rostov household.
